Strange thing about ribbon cuttings… the celebration rarely mentions how the money actually moved.

A new health center in Lee County is a real win for rural families, EMS, and the public health folks who’ve been working out of borrowed space for nearly two decades.

But the rest of the story matters, too.

And here’s what the voting record shows:

• Community Project Funding exists today because Congress restored earmarks in 2021 a reform Rep. Miller Meeks originally criticized, despite now relying on CPF to secure the $2M that made this project possible.

• The Bipartisan Appropriations Acts of 2022 and 2023, which she voted against, contained the federal health infrastructure accounts that ultimately financed CPF awards like this one.

• The 2024 House budget proposal she supported sought major cuts to HHS community health programs the same accounts that rural counties depend on to staff and sustain facilities once they’re built.

So yes, this center is good news for Lee County.

But it was federal programs she voted against that made it possible.

And now you know…the rest of the story.

@RepMMM While funding for local health services is crucial, there is a broader issue of rural hospital closures that affects community access to care. Ignoring these concerns can lead to gaps in healthcare that significantly impact families relying on these facilities.

Funny thing about rural healthcare…

Every ribbon cutting looks like progress, but the rest of the story rarely gets told.

Here’s what never gets mentioned:

• In 2021–2024, Congress received repeated GAO warnings that rural hospital closures were accelerating because Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement formulas hadn’t been updated to match actual operating costs.

• The House rejected amendments that would have expanded rural graduate medical education slots  the same shortage now forcing towns like Keokuk to rely on rotating providers instead of permanent staff.

• And in 2025, Congress allowed emergency telehealth flexibilities to lapse for several months, disrupting care in the very rural counties now struggling to rebuild access.

So yes, new clinics matter.

But no photo op changes the fact that Congress ignored the structural issues that caused these closures in the first place.

And now you know…the rest of the story.

Let's talk about your lies. Your post lies about both the Affordable Care Act and the impact of your proposal.

The ACA does not funnel taxpayer dollars to insurance companies while families suffer. Subsidies go to patients to make coverage affordable, not to insurers as profit. Insurers only receive payment if they actually cover someone, and they are legally required to spend 80 to 85 percent of premiums on medical care or issue refunds. That structure exists specifically to prevent profiteering. Higher deductibles and copays are driven by underlying healthcare costs like hospital consolidation, drug pricing, and employer plan design, not by the ACA. The law also added out of pocket caps, banned junk plans, and guaranteed coverage for people with pre existing conditions.

Just as important, the ACA is the reason more Americans have health insurance today than at any point in U.S. history. Tens of millions gained coverage through Medicaid expansion, the marketplaces, and consumer protections that made insurance accessible instead of exclusionary. That is not a side effect, it is the core success of the law.

Your plan moves the country backward. By cutting subsidies and promoting thinner coverage, it reduces affordability and shrinks the insurance pool. When healthier people are pushed out or into skimpier plans, premiums rise for everyone who remains insured. Fewer Americans can afford coverage, and the uninsured rate goes up. That is not hypothetical, it is what happens every time these policies are tried.

As the pool shrinks, insurers raise premiums, increase deductibles, and narrow networks. Families who are insured today pay more for less coverage and face higher out of pocket costs when they actually need care. Claims of expanded choice mask the reality that people are being priced out.

Your assurances about protecting people with pre existing conditions are also misleading. Coverage that exists on paper but is unaffordable or excludes key benefits is not real protection. People with cancer, diabetes, heart disease, pregnancy related needs, and chronic conditions are the first to be harmed.

The ACA expanded coverage and made healthcare attainable for more Americans than ever before. Your proposal would reverse that progress, raise costs for insured families, weaken real protections, and leave fewer Americans able to afford health insurance. Calling that reform does not make it true.
